method: Lectio Edition (SDIT): clear modern English of Dante, synthesized from the public-domain translation tradition (Longfellow 1867; Cary 1814; Norton's prose 1892) and checked against the Italian; modern verse translations consulted, not quoted. Verse lines kept. In progress, canto by canto.
sourcesCited: Charles Eliot Norton, prose (1892, public domain)
modern verse translations (Ciardi, Mandelbaum, Hollander, consulted, not quoted)
overview: The Lectio Edition renders Dante in clear modern English that keeps the forward pull of the journey and the sharpness of his images, without the inversions and archaism of the older verse. Kept line by line, canticle by canticle.
introduction: Longfellow's 1867 Dante is faithful and grave, but its nineteenth-century inversions slow a modern reader. The Lectio Edition keeps Dante's line-by-line structure and his concrete, startling imagery — the dark wood, the gates of Hell, the souls like autumn leaves — in English that moves the way Dante moves. The older verse translations and the Italian are a tap away.

divergences.phrase: selva oscura
divergences.older: a forest dark (Longfellow); a gloomy wood (Cary)
divergences.lectio: a dark wood
divergences.note: Longfellow's inverted 'a forest dark' is the kind of nineteenth-century word-order that trips a modern reader; the Italian is plainly noun-then-adjective, 'dark wood.' We keep it concrete and unadorned — it is the canto's master image.

divergences.phrase: là dove 'l sol tace
divergences.older: where the sun is silent (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the place where the sun is silent
divergences.note: Dante writes that the sun is silent, not merely dark — a deliberate crossing of senses (a place where light has gone so dead it has no voice). We keep the strangeness rather than tidy it into 'where the sun never shines.'

divergences.phrase: tra feltro e feltro
divergences.older: 'Twixt Feltro and Feltro (Longfellow); 'Twixt either Feltro (Cary)
divergences.lectio: between felt and felt
divergences.note: The veltro's (Greyhound's) birthplace is one of the most debated lines in the poem — whether 'feltro' means the towns Feltre and Montefeltro, humble felt cloth, or something else. The line is meant to be a riddle, so we keep it as a riddle rather than resolve it for the reader.

divergences.phrase: Beatrice am I, who do bid thee go
divergences.older: I am Beatrice, who do bid thee go; / I come from there, where I would fain return; / Love moved me, which compelleth me to speak.
divergences.lectio: I am Beatrice, who send you on this. / I come from the place I long to return to. / Love moved me, and makes me speak.
divergences.note: Italian 'Amor mi mosse, che mi fa parlare' — the engine of the whole rescue is love, stated plainly. We keep the simple subject 'Love' so it lands as a force, not a flourish, and drop 'fain'/'compelleth.'

divergences.phrase: I not Aeneas am, I am not Paul
divergences.older: I not Aeneas am, I am not Paul, / Nor I, nor others, think me worthy of it.
divergences.lectio: I am not Aeneas, I am not Paul. / Neither I nor anyone thinks me worthy of it.
divergences.note: Dante's 'Io non Enea, io non Paulo sono' is two stark, parallel denials — the hinge of the canto's self-doubt. We straighten Longfellow's inverted word order so the repetition hits like the original's, with nothing between the reader and the names.

divergences.phrase: the smallest of the heavens
divergences.older: all contained / Within the heaven that has the lesser circles
divergences.lectio: all that the smallest of the heavens holds
divergences.note: 'Il ciel c'ha minor li cerchi sui' is the sphere of the Moon, whose orbit is smallest — i.e., everything beneath the heavens, the whole sublunary world. We name the cosmology plainly rather than reproduce Longfellow's 'lesser circles,' which leaves a modern reader guessing.

divergences.phrase: Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch'intrate
divergences.older: All hope abandon, ye who enter in! (Longfellow); All hope abandon, ye who enter here (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Abandon every hope, you who enter here.
divergences.note: The most famous line carved over Hell's gate. Longfellow's inverted 'All hope abandon, ye who enter in' is exactly the archaic word-order The Vernacular removes. The Italian is a plain, terrible imperative — verb, object, then the address — so we keep it that way: 'Abandon every hope.' We say 'every' (ogne) rather than 'all,' since Dante stresses each separate hope being given up, and 'here' for the gate the reader is standing at.

divergences.phrase: che fece per viltade il gran rifiuto
divergences.older: Who made through cowardice the great refusal (Longfellow); who in his cowardice / Made the great refusal (Cary)
divergences.lectio: who out of cowardice made the great refusal
divergences.note: Dante deliberately leaves this shade unnamed — most readers take it for Pope Celestine V, who abdicated the papacy, but the poem will not say so. We keep the figure anonymous and keep the resonant phrase 'the great refusal' intact rather than explaining it, because the withholding is the point.

divergences.phrase: Come d'autunno si levan le foglie
divergences.older: As in the autumn-time the leaves fall off (Longfellow); As fall off the light autumnal leaves (Cary)
divergences.lectio: The way the leaves let go in autumn
divergences.note: The canto's central image — the dead dropping one by one into Charon's boat like falling leaves. Dante's verb is 'si levan' (lift away / let go), gentler and stranger than 'fall off.' We keep that releasing motion ('let go') so the simile carries the eerie willingness Dante gives it, matching the falling-leaves image already named in this edition's overview.

divergences.phrase: cignesi con la coda tante volte / quantunque gradi vuol che giù sia messa
divergences.older: Girds himself with his tail as many times / As grades he wishes it should be thrust down (Longfellow); Girds him with his tail. As many times / As he would have it thrust into the abyss (Cary)
divergences.lectio: coils his tail around himself as many times / as the number of circles it must be flung down
divergences.note: Minos, the infernal judge, assigns each soul its circle by the grotesque mechanism of winding his tail: the number of coils is the number of the circle. Longfellow's 'girds himself' and 'grades' obscure the physical image. We keep the concrete, animal motion — a tail coiling — and name 'circles' plainly, since that is what the count means for a reader following the descent.

divergences.phrase: Amor, ch'al cor gentil ratto s'apprende ... Amor, ch'a nullo amato amar perdona ... Amor condusse noi ad una morte
divergences.older: Love, that on gentle heart doth swiftly seize ... Love, that exempts no one beloved from loving ... Love has conducted us unto one death (Longfellow); Love, that in gentle heart is quickly learnt ... Love, that denial takes from none beloved ... Love brought us to one death (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Love, which is quick to seize the gentle heart ... Love, which absolves no loved one from loving ... Love led the two of us to a single death.
divergences.note: Francesca's three tercets each open with 'Amor' — an anaphora that is the rhetorical heart of the canto and a deliberate echo of the courtly-love doctrine (Guinizzelli's 'al cor gentil') Dante is at once moved by and judging. We preserve all three 'Love' openings so the drumbeat survives in English, and keep the famous middle line's terrible symmetry — to be loved is to be condemned to love back ('absolves no loved one from loving') — without untangling it into prose. Longfellow's 'exempts' is legalistic but cold; 'absolves' keeps the religious weight Dante sets against this love.

divergences.phrase: Galeotto fu 'l libro e chi lo scrisse
divergences.older: Galeotto was the book and he who wrote it (Longfellow); The book and writer both / Were love's purveyors (Cary)
divergences.lectio: A Galeotto was that book, and the one who wrote it.
divergences.note: In the Lancelot romance Paolo and Francesca were reading, Galehaut (Italian Galeotto) is the go-between who brings Lancelot and Guinevere together — so 'Galeotto' had become an Italian word for a pander, a love's-procurer. Dante's line says the book itself, and its author, played that role for them. We keep the proper noun 'Galeotto' (the architecture of the allusion) but cast it as 'a Galeotto,' so the reader feels it working as the title it has become: the book was their go-between. Cary's 'love's purveyors' explains the pun but loses the name; Longfellow keeps the name but leaves a modern reader stranded. Our phrasing keeps both.

divergences.phrase: 'l maestro di color che sanno
divergences.older: The Master of those who know (Longfellow); the master of the sapient throng (Cary)
divergences.lectio: the master of those who know
divergences.note: Dante's famous title for Aristotle — never named, only honored as the one who masters all knowing. The Italian is plain and absolute: 'the master of those who know.' We keep it exactly, without naming Aristotle for the reader, because the withholding of the name is part of the reverence — to a medieval mind he simply was 'the Philosopher.'

divergences.phrase: un possente, con segno di vittoria coronato
divergences.older: a Mighty One, / With sign of victory incoronate (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: a Mighty One ... crowned with the sign of victory
divergences.note: This is the Harrowing of Hell — Christ descending to free the patriarchs — but Dante, in Virgil's pagan mouth, will not say the name. He gives only 'un possente,' a powerful one, crowned with victory. We keep that veiling ('a Mighty One') and drop Longfellow's Latinate 'incoronate,' since the point is a power Virgil witnessed but could not name.

divergences.phrase: sanza speme vivemo in disio
divergences.older: without hope we live on in desire (Longfellow); we without hope live on in longing (Cary)
divergences.lectio: with no hope, we go on living in longing
divergences.note: The whole sentence of Limbo in five words: not fire, not torment, but desire that can never be answered. We keep the bare antithesis Dante builds — hope set against longing — rather than soften it, because that ache is the precise punishment of the virtuous unbaptized, and the canto turns on it.

divergences.phrase: la parte selvaggia ... colui che testé piaggia
divergences.older: the rustic party / Will drive the other out (Longfellow); the savage part / Shall scatter forth the other (Cary)
divergences.lectio: the party from the woods will drive the other out ... by the power of one who now plays both shores
divergences.note: Ciacco's prophecy is deliberately veiled, and Dante's first readers had to decode it: 'la parte selvaggia' is the White Guelphs (Dante's own side, cast as the 'rustic' or 'woodland' party because its leaders came from the contado), and 'colui che testé piaggia' — literally 'the one who now hugs the coast,' i.e. temporizes, plays both sides — is Pope Boniface VIII, whose backing would restore the Blacks. We keep the veil rather than naming Boniface, because the riddling indirection is the canto's politics; but we render 'piaggia' with its concrete nautical image, 'plays both shores,' instead of Longfellow's flat 'is on the coast.'

divergences.phrase: Giusti son due, e non vi sono intesi; / superbia, invidia e avarizia sono / le tre faville c'hanno i cuori accesi
divergences.older: The just are two, and are not understood there; / Envy and Arrogance and Avarice / Are the three sparks (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: The just are two, and no one there will hear them. / Pride, envy, and greed are the three sparks / that have set every heart on fire.
divergences.note: Dante names the three sins in a fixed order — superbia, invidia, avarizia (pride, envy, avarice) — that he returns to across the poem; Longfellow reshuffles them to 'Envy and Arrogance and Avarice,' losing both the order and the plain word 'pride.' We restore Dante's sequence. And 'non vi sono intesi' is not 'not understood' but 'not heeded, not listened to' — the just men are there but no one in Florence pays them any mind — so we render it 'no one there will hear them.'

divergences.phrase: Ritorna a tua scïenza ... quanto la cosa è più perfetta, / più senta il bene, e così la doglienza
divergences.older: Return unto thy science, / Which wills, that as the thing more perfect is, / The more it feels of pleasure and of pain (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Go back to your science, which holds that the more perfect a thing is, / the more it feels of pleasure and of pain.
divergences.note: Virgil sends Dante back to 'tua scïenza' — Aristotle, the philosophy Dante studied — for the canto's hard doctrine: after the Last Judgment the damned will be reunited with their bodies and so made more complete, and a more perfect being feels everything more keenly, suffering included. The thought is genuinely difficult and we keep it difficult; we only strip Longfellow's archaic 'which wills, that as the thing more perfect is' down to a clause a modern reader can follow, without softening the chilling conclusion that being made whole makes the pain worse.

divergences.phrase: Pape Satàn, pape Satàn aleppe
divergences.older: Pape Satan, Pape Satan, Aleppe! (Longfellow); Ah me! O Satan! Satan! (Cary, who attempts a paraphrase)
divergences.lectio: Pape Satàn, pape Satàn aleppe!
divergences.note: Plutus's opening cry is one of the famous puzzles of the poem — a line of garbled, half-infernal language that no one has ever convincingly translated, and that Dante surely meant to be unintelligible (a few lines later he calls it the 'voce chioccia,' the clucking, strangled voice). Cary tried to make sense of it; Longfellow wisely left it alone. We keep it untouched in the Italian, accents and all, so the reader meets exactly what Dante meant them to meet: noise that means menace without meaning words.

divergences.phrase: Taci, maladetto lupo
divergences.older: Be silent, thou accursed wolf (Longfellow); Peace, cursed wolf (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Be quiet, you cursed wolf.
divergences.note: Virgil silences Plutus by calling him a wolf — the same animal as the she-wolf of greed from Canto I, the beast of insatiable appetite — which fixes this whole circle as the place of avarice before a single hoarder is named. We keep the plain, hard noun 'wolf' rather than softening it, and let 'cursed' carry its full force, because the insult is doing the work of an exorcism.

divergences.phrase: là dove Michele / fé la vendetta del superbo strupo
divergences.older: where Michael wrought / Vengeance upon the proud adultery (Longfellow); where Michael wreak'd / Vengeance upon the proud adultery (Cary)
divergences.lectio: there where Michael / took his vengeance on the proud rebellion.
divergences.note: Dante's 'superbo strupo' refers to the war in Heaven, where the archangel Michael cast down the rebel angels. 'Strupo' is an old, violent word (a doublet of stupro, ravishment / violation), and the older translators render it 'adultery,' which lands strangely on a modern ear and obscures the event. The sin being punished is pride — angels who 'violated' the order of Heaven by revolting. We render it 'the proud rebellion' so a reader instantly knows what Michael's vengeance was for, while keeping 'proud' (superbo), which names the sin.

divergences.phrase: Perché tieni? / Perché burli?
divergences.older: "Why keepest?" and, "Why squanderest thou?" (Longfellow); "Why holdest thou?" "Why throwest away?" (Cary)
divergences.lectio: "Why hoard?" and "Why throw it away?"
divergences.note: The two crowds rolling weights against each other are the hoarders and the spendthrifts, and the entire logic of their punishment is in these two shouted accusations they hurl as they collide — each crowd condemning the other's vice. We keep the curt, taunting two-beat rhythm of the original ('Perché tieni? / Perché burli?'), so the reader hears the eternal argument as a clash and not a translation.

divergences.phrase: ordinò general ministra e duce
divergences.older: Ordained a general ministress and guide (Longfellow); appointed her his general minister and guide (Cary)
divergences.lectio: he set a general minister and guide
divergences.note: Virgil's whole defense of Fortune turns on this word: she is not blind chance but a 'minister' — an angelic intelligence God appointed to govern the shifting of worldly goods, ranked among the other heavenly powers ('the other gods,' as he puts it). We keep 'minister and guide' to preserve that she is an officeholder under God, not a capricious idol; the point of the passage is that mortals curse her wrongly. (See the companion note at VII.91 on 'crucified.')

divergences.phrase: Quest' è colei ch'è tanto posta in croce
divergences.older: And this is she who is so crucified (Longfellow); This is she so reviled (often softened in prose)
divergences.lectio: And this is the one so often nailed to the cross
divergences.note: Dante uses 'posta in croce' — literally put on the cross, crucified — for the abuse people heap on Fortune, a deliberately shocking word that casts her as wrongly condemned, even martyred, by the very people who profit from her. We keep the crucifixion image ('nailed to the cross') rather than flattening it to 'reviled' or 'blamed,' because the violence of the metaphor is the point: those who should praise her instead crucify her with their cursing, and she, blessed, does not even hear it.

divergences.phrase: le sue meschite
divergences.older: Its mosques (Longfellow); the mosques (Cary)
divergences.lectio: its mosques
divergences.note: Dante calls the buildings of the infernal city 'meschite' — mosques — because to a medieval Christian the mosque was the architecture of the enemy faith, so the word marks Dis as utterly hostile ground. The image is strange to a modern reader, but we keep 'mosques' rather than soften it to 'towers' or 'temples,' because the strangeness is the point: this is how Dante's world saw the citadel of the damned.

divergences.phrase: Con piangere e con lutto ... spirito maladetto, ti rimani
divergences.older: With weeping and with wailing, / Thou spirit maledict, do thou remain (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: With your weeping and your wailing, / you cursed spirit, stay right where you are
divergences.note: This is the harsh exchange with Filippo Argenti, and Dante's contempt is meant to be felt, not smoothed. We straighten Longfellow's inverted 'do thou remain' and archaic 'maledict' into plain, cutting modern speech, so the reader hears the cold satisfaction the pilgrim takes in the man's torment — a hardness Dante deliberately stages and Virgil then blesses.

divergences.phrase: le porte ... ne richiusero
divergences.older: They closed the portals, those our adversaries, / On my Lord's breast (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: They slammed the gates, those enemies of ours, / in my lord's face
divergences.note: The fallen angels shut Hell's inner gate against Virgil — the poem's guide, who has never before been refused. Longfellow's 'closed the portals ... on my Lord's breast' is grave but slack. We render the verb hard ('slammed') and put the door 'in his face,' because the humiliation is the dramatic hinge of the canto: even Virgil's authority fails here, and only the coming heavenly messenger will open the way.

divergences.phrase: O voi ch'avete li 'ntelletti sani, / mirate la dottrina che s'asconde / sotto 'l velame de li versi strani
divergences.older: O ye who have undistempered intellects, / Observe the doctrine that conceals itself / Beneath the veil of the mysterious verses! (Longfellow); O ye of sound intellect, mark well the lore / Conceal'd under the veil of strange verse (Cary)
divergences.lectio: O you who have sound and steady minds, / look hard at the teaching that hides itself / beneath the veil of these strange verses.
divergences.note: Dante's most direct address to the reader, breaking the frame to say outright that this scene is an allegory with a hidden meaning. The Italian 'intelletti sani' means healthy, sound minds, not Longfellow's clinical 'undistempered intellects.' We keep the famous metaphor 'veil of strange verses' (velame de li versi strani) intact rather than explaining what lies under it — the whole point of the tercet is that Dante refuses to lift the veil for us, and so do we.

divergences.phrase: passando per lo Stige con le piante asciutte
divergences.older: Was passing o'er the Styx with soles unwet (Longfellow); o'er the Stygian ferry pass'd with unwet feet (Cary)
divergences.lectio: crossing the Styx on foot, his soles never touching the water
divergences.note: The heaven-sent messenger walks dry-shod across the swamp that the damned must wade or be ferried through — a quiet, deliberate miracle that marks him as belonging to a different order entirely. Longfellow's 'soles unwet' is exact but archaic and easy to skim past; we slow the image down ('his soles never touching the water') so the reader registers the wonder of it, since the dry feet are the whole sign of his power.

divergences.phrase: con una verghetta
divergences.older: with a little rod / He opened it (Longfellow); with a wand he touch'd / The gate (Cary)
divergences.lectio: with a little wand he opened it, and nothing held against him
divergences.note: The messenger opens the iron-barred gates of Dis that defeated Virgil with nothing but a 'verghetta' — a slender wand or twig — and meets no resistance ('sanza alcun contasto'). We keep the diminutive ('a little wand') because the contrast is the meaning: the gate that all of Hell's demons held shut against the poets gives way to a touch. We render 'non v'ebbe alcun contasto' as 'nothing held against him,' plainer than Longfellow's 'there was no resistance,' so the effortlessness lands.

divergences.phrase: com'avesse l'inferno a gran dispitto
divergences.older: E'en as if Hell he had in great despite (Longfellow); As if he entertain'd / Great scorn of hell (Cary)
divergences.lectio: as if he held all Hell in great contempt
divergences.note: The defining image of Farinata — the proud Ghibelline leader rising erect from the burning tomb. Dante's 'a gran dispitto' is plain and total: not flinching scorn but settled, towering contempt for the whole place that holds him. Longfellow's archaic 'in great despite' has dropped out of living English, so we render it 'in great contempt' and keep 'all Hell' so the defiance is aimed at the entirety of his damnation, which is the point of the man.

divergences.phrase: dicesti "elli ebbe"? non viv'elli ancora?
divergences.older: Saidst thou,—he had? Is he not still alive? (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: You said held — held? Is he not still alive?
divergences.note: The hinge of Cavalcante's collapse. Dante said his guide led him perhaps to one Guido 'ebbe a disdegno' — used the past tense 'ebbe' (held) — and the grieving father seizes on that one verb, reading his son's death into it. Everything turns on a tense, so the English must put the same word under the same stress; we isolate and repeat 'held' (matching the 'disdain' verb three tercets up) rather than Longfellow's vaguer 'he had,' so a modern reader feels exactly what the father heard.

divergences.phrase: non cinquanta volte fia raccesa / la faccia de la donna che qui regge
divergences.older: But fifty times shall not rekindled be / The countenance of the Lady who reigns here (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the face of the lady who reigns down here / will not be rekindled fifty times
divergences.note: Farinata's prophecy of Dante's exile, given as a riddle of time. 'The lady who reigns here' is the moon — Proserpina/Hecate, queen of the underworld, identified with the moon — so 'fifty kindlings of her face' means fifty new moons, about four years, before Dante himself learns 'how heavy that art is' (the art of returning from exile). We keep the veil exactly as Dante leaves it — a named goddess only by epithet, her 'face' the lunar disk relit each month — rather than flatten it to 'fifty months,' because the prophecy is meant to be decoded, not handed over.

books.label: Inferno: Canto I
paragraphs:
Midway along the journey of our life
I came to myself in a dark wood,
for the straight road had been lost.

How hard it is to say what it was like —
that wood, so wild and rough and unrelenting
the fear comes back the moment I think of it.

It was so bitter that death is hardly worse.
But to tell of the good I found there too,
I'll speak of the other things I saw.

How I came to enter it I can't say clearly,
so heavy was I with sleep at the moment
I wandered off from the true way.

But once I had reached the foot of a hill,
there where the valley came to an end
that had pierced my heart with dread,

I looked up and saw its shoulders
already wrapped in that planet's rays
that lead us straight down every road.

Then the fear grew a little quieter
that had lasted through the lake of my heart
all that night I'd spent in such misery.

And like a man who, gasping for breath,
drags himself out of the sea onto the shore
and turns to stare back at the dangerous water,

so my mind, still racing in flight,
turned back to look again at that pass
no living person has ever left.

After I had rested my worn-out body
I took up the climb again on the empty slope,
my lower foot always the steady one.

And there, almost where the climb began,
a leopard — quick and very light on its feet,
its coat all covered in spots —

would not move out of my path.
It blocked my way so completely
that again and again I turned to go back.

It was the early hour of morning,
and the sun was climbing with the same stars
that rode beside it when Divine Love

first set those beautiful things in motion.
So the hour of the day and the sweet season
gave me good reason to hope

even against that beast with its bright pelt —
but not enough to keep me from fear
when a lion came into view.

It looked like it was coming straight at me,
head high, in a fury of hunger,
until the very air seemed afraid of it.

And a she-wolf, who in her gauntness
seemed loaded down with every craving
and has made so many live in grief —

she laid such a weight on me,
such terror came off the sight of her,
that I gave up all hope of the height.

And like a man who gladly piles up gains,
but when the time comes that he loses them
weeps and despairs in all his thoughts,

that restless beast did the same to me:
coming on, pushing me back step by step
toward the place where the sun is silent.

While I was sliding down toward the low ground,
before my eyes someone appeared
who seemed faint, hoarse from long silence.

When I saw him there in the vast waste,
"Have pity on me," I cried out to him,
"whatever you are — a shade, or a real man."

He answered: "Not a man. I was one once.
My parents both came from Lombardy,
Mantuans, both of them, by birth.

I was born under Julius, though late in his day,
and lived at Rome under the good Augustus,
in the time of the false and lying gods.

I was a poet, and I sang of that just
son of Anchises who came out of Troy
after proud Ilion was burned to the ground.

But you — why turn back to all that misery?
Why not climb the mountain of delight,
the source and cause of every joy?"

"Then are you that Virgil, that fountain
that pours out so wide a river of speech?"
I answered him, my head bowed in shame.

"You, the honor and the light of all the other poets —
let the long study and the great love
that drove me to your book stand for me now.

You are my master, you are my author.
You alone are the one from whom I took
the noble style that has earned me my name.

Look at the beast that turned me back.
Save me from her, famous sage,
for she sets my veins and pulses shaking."

"You have to go another way,"
he answered, when he saw me weeping,
"if you want to escape this wild place,

because this beast that makes you cry out
lets no one pass along her road,
but harries him until she kills him.

Her nature is so cruel, so vicious,
that she never fills her greedy appetite —
after feeding she's hungrier than before.

Many are the animals she mates with,
and more there'll be, until the Greyhound comes
who will hunt her down to a painful death.

He won't feed on land or money,
but on wisdom, on love and courage,
and his birthplace will lie between felt and felt.

Through every city he'll drive her down,
until he's chased her back into Hell,
out of which envy first turned her loose.

And so, for your own good, I judge it best
that you follow me. I'll be your guide,
and lead you out of here through an eternal place,

where you'll hear the cries of the hopeless,
where you'll see the ancient spirits in their grief,
each one screaming for a second death.

And then you'll see those who are content
within the fire, because they hope to come,
whenever it may be, among the blessed.

because that Emperor who reigns above —
since I rebelled against his law —
wills that none come through me into his city.

He governs everywhere, but he rules from there.
There is his city and his high throne.
Happy the one he chooses for it!"

And I said to him: "Poet, I beg you,
by that same God you never knew,
so that I escape this evil and worse,

lead me to the place you spoke of,
so I may see the gate of Saint Peter
and those you call so wretched."
Then he set out, and I followed behind.

books.label: Inferno: Canto II
paragraphs:
The day was leaving, and the darkening air
was letting the creatures of the earth
rest from their labors; I alone

was making myself ready for the struggle —
the hard road and the suffering both —
which memory, which does not fail, will trace again.

O Muses, O high genius, help me now.
O memory, that wrote down what I saw,
here your true worth will show.

I began: "Poet, you who guide me,
look at my courage — is it enough,
before you trust me to this brutal pass?

But if the enemy of all evil
was gracious to him, thinking of the great effect
that would come of it — who he was, and what —

and that empire, if we want the truth,
was founded as the holy place
where the heir of greatest Peter sits.

On this journey you give him such credit for,
he heard the things that were the cause
both of his victory and of the papal robe.

Later the Chosen Vessel went there too,
to bring back proof for that Faith
which is the first step on salvation's road.

But I — why would I go? Who grants it?
I am not Aeneas, I am not Paul.
Neither I nor anyone thinks me worthy of it.

So if I give myself up to this coming,
I'm afraid the coming may be folly.
You are wise; you understand better than I can say."

And like a man who unwills what he willed,
and on second thought changes his intention
so that he backs out of it completely,

that's what I became on that dark slope:
by thinking I burned up the whole undertaking
that had been so quick to start.

"If I have understood your words rightly,"
answered that shade of the great soul,
"your spirit is touched with cowardice,

which often weighs a man down so
it turns him back from a worthy enterprise,
the way a trick of the eye spooks a shying beast.

To free you from this fear,
I'll tell you why I came, and what I heard
the first moment I felt pity for you.

I was among those who hang in suspense
when a lady called to me, so fair, so holy
that I begged her to command me.

Her eyes shone brighter than the stars,
and she began, gentle and low,
in an angel's voice, in her own tongue:

'O courteous spirit of Mantua,
whose fame still lasts in the world
and will last as long as the world goes on,

a friend of mine — not a friend of fortune —
is blocked on the empty hillside
so badly that he has turned back in terror,

and may already be so lost, I fear,
that I have risen too late to help him,
from what I've heard of him in Heaven.

Go now, and with your polished speech
and whatever else he needs to get free,
help him, so that I am consoled.

I am Beatrice, who send you on this.
I come from the place I long to return to.
Love moved me, and makes me speak.

When I stand again before my Lord,
I'll praise you to him often.'
Then she fell silent, and I began:

'O lady of virtue, you alone
through whom the human race rises above
all that the smallest of the heavens holds,

your command pleases me so much
that to obey, even if already done, would feel late.
You need say nothing more of what you want.

But tell me why you don't shrink
from coming down here into this center
from the wide place you burn to go back to.'

'Since you so deeply want to understand,
I'll tell you briefly,' she answered me,
'why I'm not afraid to enter here.

The only things one ought to fear
are those that have the power to harm.
The rest, no — they are nothing to dread.

God in his mercy made me such
that your misery does not touch me,
nor any flame of this burning reach me.

A gentle lady is in Heaven who grieves
at this hard place I'm sending you to,
so that strict judgment up above is bent.

She called Lucia and made her plea:
'Your faithful one is in need of you now,
and I commend him to your care.'

Lucia, the enemy of all that's cruel,
rose and came to where I sat
with ancient Rachel at my side.

'Beatrice,' she said, 'true praise of God,
why don't you help the man who loved you so
that for you he left the common crowd?

Don't you hear how pitiful his weeping is?
Don't you see the death that fights him
beside a flood the sea itself can't boast of?'

No one in the world ever moved so fast
to seize their good or flee their harm
as I did, after those words were spoken.

I came down here from my blessed seat,
trusting in your honest, dignified speech,
which honors you and all who've listened to it.'

After she had spoken to me this way,
weeping, she turned her shining eyes aside,
and that made me all the quicker to come.

And so I came to you, as she wished.
I took you out of the path of that wild beast
that blocked the short climb up the lovely mountain.

So what is it? Why, why do you hold back?
Why let such cowardice nest in your heart?
Why don't you have the daring and the nerve,

when three such blessed ladies
are caring for you in the court of Heaven,
and my own words promise you so much good?"

Like little flowers, bent down and shut
by the night's chill, that lift themselves
all open on their stems once the sun whitens them,

that's what I became, with my worn-out strength,
and so much courage poured into my heart
that I began, like a man set free of fear:

"O she of such compassion, who came to my aid,
and you, so gracious, who obeyed at once
the words of truth she gave you —

Go now — one single will moves both of us.
You are my leader, my lord, my master."
So I told him; and when he started off,
I entered on the deep and savage way.

books.label: Inferno: Canto III
paragraphs:
"Through me you go to the city of grief.
Through me you go to everlasting pain.
Through me you go among the people who are lost.

Justice moved my maker on high.
Divine power made me,
the highest wisdom, and the first love.

Before me nothing was created
but things eternal, and I last forever.
Abandon every hope, you who enter here."

These words, in a dark color, I saw
carved over the top of a gate.
I said: "Master, their meaning is hard for me."

And he, like one who already knew, replied:
"Here you must let go of every doubt.
Every cowardice must die here.

We have come to the place I told you of,
where you will see the suffering people
who have lost the good of the mind."

And then he laid his hand on mine,
with a calm, glad look that steadied me,
and led me in among the hidden things.

There sighs and weeping and loud wailing
rang through the starless air,
so that at first I wept to hear it.

Strange tongues, monstrous accents,
words of pain, voices of fury,
high cries and hoarse ones, and the smack of hands —

all of it made a tumult that wheels on
forever through that air forever black,
the way sand swirls up when the whirlwind blows.

And I, my head ringed round with horror,
said: "Master, what is this I'm hearing?
Who are these people so broken by their pain?"

And he to me: "This wretched way of being
belongs to the dreary souls of those
who lived with no disgrace and no praise.

They are mixed in with that worthless choir
of angels who were neither rebels
nor faithful to God, but only for themselves.

Heaven cast them out, to keep its beauty pure,
and the depths of Hell won't take them either,
since the damned would find some glory next to them."

And I: "Master, what weighs on them so hard
that it makes them cry out like this?"
He answered: "I'll tell you, and keep it short.

These have no hope of ever dying,
and their blind life is so debased
they envy every other fate there is.

The world allows no memory of them.
Mercy and justice both look down on them.
Let's not talk about them — look, and move on."

And I, looking again, saw a banner
that ran in circles, spinning so fast
it seemed to scorn the thought of ever stopping.

And behind it came so long a line
of people, I would never have believed
that death had undone so many.

When I had recognized a few of them,
I looked, and I saw the shade of the one
who out of cowardice made the great refusal.

At once I understood, and I was sure,
that this was the crowd of worthless souls
hateful to God and to his enemies alike.

These wretches, who were never truly alive,
were naked, and were stung again and again
by the wasps and hornets swarming there.

The stings streaked their faces with blood
that ran down, mixed with their tears,
and was gathered at their feet by loathsome worms.

And when I turned to look still farther on,
I saw people along the bank of a great river,
and I said: "Master, tell me now,

so I may know who these are, and what law
makes them seem so eager to cross over,
as far as I can tell in this dim light."

And he to me: "All this will be made clear
to you, the moment we stop and stand
on the dismal shore of Acheron."

Then, with my eyes lowered in shame,
afraid my words had begun to annoy him,
I held my tongue until we reached the river.

And look — coming toward us in a boat,
an old man, white with the hair of age,
shouting: "Misery on you, you ruined souls!

Give up all hope of ever seeing the sky.
I come to carry you to the other shore,
into the eternal dark, the heat and frost.

And you over there — you, the living soul —
get away from these, for they are dead."
But when he saw that I would not go,

he said: "By another way, another port
you'll reach the shore to cross, not here.
A lighter craft will have to carry you."

And my guide: "Charon, don't fight it.
This is willed where what is willed is done,
so ask no more."

At that, the shaggy cheeks went still
on the ferryman of the livid swamp,
who had wheels of flame around his eyes.

But those souls, worn out and naked,
went pale and ground their teeth together
the moment they heard the cruel words.

They cursed God and cursed their parents,
the whole human race, the place, the time,
the seed they sprang from, the day they were born.

Then all of them drew back together,
weeping bitterly, toward the cursed shore
that waits for every man who does not fear God.

Charon the demon, with eyes like burning coals,
signals to them and herds them all aboard,
beating with his oar any soul that lags.

The way the leaves let go in autumn,
one after another, until the branch
sees all its riches lying on the ground —

just so the evil seed of Adam
throw themselves down from that bank one by one,
at his signal, like a bird answering its call.

So they go off across the dark water,
and before they have landed on the far side,
a fresh crowd is already gathering on this one.

"My son," the gentle master said to me,
"all those who die under the wrath of God
come together here from every land.

And they are eager to cross the river,
because the justice of Heaven drives them on
until their fear is turned into desire.

No good soul ever passes this way.
So if Charon complains about you,
you can understand now what his words mean."

When he had finished, the whole dark plain
shook so violently that even now
the memory of that terror bathes me in sweat.

The land of tears let out a blast of wind
that flared with a flash of crimson light,
and it overcame every sense in me,
and I fell, like a man taken by sleep.

books.label: Inferno: Canto IV
paragraphs:
A heavy crash of thunder broke the deep
sleep in my head, and I came to with a start,
like someone shaken awake by force.

I stood up straight, my body rested now,
and turned my eyes around, fully awake,
to make out where it was I had come to.

The truth is, I found myself on the very edge
of the valley of grief, that bottomless abyss
where the thunder of endless wailing gathers.

It was so dark, so deep and full of mist
that however hard I fixed my eyes on its floor,
I could make out nothing down there at all.

"Now let us go down into the blind world,"
the poet began, and his face had gone white.
"I will go first, and you will come behind."

And I, who saw the color drain from him,
said: "How am I to go, if you're afraid —
you, who have always steadied me in my fear?"

And he to me: "It's the anguish of the people
down here that paints my face the way you see,
and you have taken that pity for terror.

Let's go. The long road won't wait for us."
And so he went in, and led me in with him,
to the first circle that rings the abyss.

There, as far as I could tell by listening,
there was no weeping, no — only sighs,
that set the everlasting air trembling.

And this came out of grief without torment,
the grief of the crowds — and they were many, and great —
of little children, and women, and men.

The good master said to me: "You don't ask
who these spirits are that you're looking at?
I want you to know, before you go on,

that they didn't sin; and whatever good they did,
it isn't enough, because they were not baptized,
the gateway into the faith you hold.

And those who came before Christianity
did not worship God in the right way.
And I myself am one of them.

For that lack, and for no other guilt,
we are lost, and our only punishment is this:
with no hope, we go on living in longing."

Great grief took hold of my heart when I heard him,
because I knew some people of real worth
who hung suspended in that Limbo.

"Tell me, my master — tell me, my lord,"
I began, wanting to be certain now
of the faith that overcomes every error,

"did anyone ever leave here — by his own merit,
or by another's — and go on to be blessed?"
And he, who caught the thing I couldn't say outright,

answered: "I was still new to this place
when I saw a Mighty One come down to us,
crowned with the sign of victory.

He drew out the shade of our first father,
and of his son Abel, and of Noah,
of Moses the lawgiver, the obedient

Abraham, the patriarch, and David the king,
Israel, with his father and his sons,
and Rachel, the one he had labored so long for,

and many more, and he made them blessed.
And you should know that before these souls,
no human spirit had ever been saved."

We did not stop walking while he spoke,
but kept moving on the whole time through the forest —
the forest, I mean, of crowded ghosts.

Our way had not yet carried us far
this side of where I'd slept, when I saw a fire
that won back a hemisphere from the dark.

We were still some distance off from it,
but not so far that I couldn't partly see
that people of honor held that place.

"You who honor every art and science,
who are these, with such great honor
that it sets them apart from all the rest?"

And he to me: "The honored name of them
that still rings of them up in your life
wins grace in Heaven, which raises them like this."

Just then I heard a voice ring out:
"All honor to the greatest of the poets!
His shade, which had gone, is coming back."

After the voice had stopped and gone still,
I saw four great shades coming toward us.
Their faces were neither sorrowful nor glad.

My gracious master began to speak to me:
"Look at the one with the sword in his hand,
who comes ahead of the three, like their lord.

That is Homer, sovereign poet of them all.
The next to come is Horace, the satirist.
The third is Ovid, and the last is Lucan.

Because each one of them shares with me
the name that single voice just cried aloud,
they do me honor, and they do well in it."

And so I saw them gather, the fair school
of that lord of the highest song,
who soars above the others like an eagle.

After they had talked among themselves a while,
they turned to me with a sign of welcome,
and my master smiled to see it.

And they did me still greater honor than that:
they made me one of their own company,
so that I was the sixth among such minds.

So we went on toward the light, and talked
of things it's good to keep silent about now,
as good as it was to speak of them there.

We came to the foot of a noble castle,
ringed seven times with its high walls,
and guarded all around by a lovely stream.

We crossed over this as if on solid ground.
Through seven gates I entered with those sages,
and we came out on a meadow of fresh green.

There were people there with calm, slow eyes,
great authority in the way they looked,
who spoke seldom, and in gentle voices.

We drew off together to one side,
into an open place, bright and high,
so that all of them could be seen.

There, straight ahead, on the green enamel,
the great spirits were pointed out to me,
and the sight of them still lifts me up inside.

I saw Electra with many companions,
and among them I knew Hector and Aeneas,
and Caesar, armed, with his hawk's keen eyes.

I saw Camilla and Penthesilea
on the other side, and I saw King Latinus,
seated with his daughter Lavinia.

I saw that Brutus who drove out Tarquin,
Lucretia, Julia, Marcia, and Cornelia,
and, alone and apart, I saw Saladin.

When I raised my eyes a little higher,
I saw the master of those who know,
sitting among his family of philosophers.

Democritus, who lays the world to chance,
Diogenes, Anaxagoras, and Thales,
Zeno, Empedocles, and Heraclitus.

I saw the one who gathered the powers of things,
Dioscorides, I mean; and I saw Orpheus,
Tully and Livy, and the moralist Seneca,

Euclid the geometer, and Ptolemy,
Galen, Hippocrates, and Avicenna,
and Averroes, who wrote the great Commentary.

I can't give the full account of all of them,
because the long theme drives me on so hard
that again and again the words fall short of the facts.

The company of six splits into two.
My wise guide leads me off another way,
out of the stillness into the trembling air,
and I come to a place where nothing shines.

books.label: Inferno: Canto V
paragraphs:
So I went down from the first circle
into the second, which rings a smaller space
but so much greater pain that it goads them to howling.

I mean that when a soul born to evil
comes before him, it confesses everything,
and that connoisseur of sins

sees what place in Hell is fit for it,
and coils his tail around himself as many times
as the number of circles it must be flung down.

"You there, who come to this house of grief,"
said Minos when he saw me,
breaking off from the work of his great office,

"watch how you enter, and whom you trust.
Don't let the wide gate fool you."
And my guide to him: "Why do you too cry out?

Don't block his journey — it is fated.
This is willed where what is willed is done,
so ask no more."

And now the notes of grief begin
to reach my ears; now I have come
where a great wailing beats against me.

I came into a place where all light is silent,
that bellows like the sea in a storm
when it is battered by warring winds.

The hurricane of Hell, which never rests,
drives the spirits on before its force,
wheeling and battering, it gives them no peace.

I understood that to a torment like this
the sinners of the flesh were condemned,
who let their reason give way to their hunger.

And as the wings of starlings carry them
in the cold season, in a wide, packed flock,
so that blast carries the wicked spirits:

And as the cranes go chanting their cries,
drawing themselves out in a long line through the air,
so I saw them come, wailing,

shades borne along on that same wind.
So I said: "Master, who are these people
the black air punishes so hard?"

"The first of those you want to know about,"
he said to me then,
"was empress over many tongues.

She was so broken by the vice of lust
that she made desire lawful in her code,
to wipe out the blame she had fallen into.

The next is the one who killed herself for love
and broke faith with the ashes of Sychaeus.
After her, Cleopatra, who lived for pleasure."

I saw Helen, for whom so many cruel
years wheeled round, and I saw great Achilles,
who fought with Love at the very end.

I saw Paris, Tristan — more than a thousand
shades he named and pointed out with his finger,
all the ones Love had cut away from our life.

After I had listened to my teacher
name the ladies and the knights of long ago,
pity overcame me, and I was almost lost.

I began: "Poet, I would gladly
speak to those two who go together
and seem so light upon the wind."

And he to me: "Watch for them when they come
closer to us; then call to them
by the love that drives them, and they will come."

As soon as the wind bent them toward us,
I raised my voice: "O weary souls,
come speak with us, if no one forbids it."

As doves, called onward by desire,
with wings held open and still glide
to the sweet nest, carried by their own will,

so these two left the flock where Dido is
and came to us through the malignant air,
so strong was the love in my call.

"O living creature, gracious and kind,
who come visiting through this dark air
to us who stained the world with blood,

if the King of all things were our friend
we would pray to him to give you peace,
since you take pity on our twisted grief.

Whatever you would like to hear and say,
that we will hear, and we will say to you,
while the wind, as now, is still.

The city where I was born sits
on the shore where the Po comes down
to rest in peace with all the streams that follow it.

Love, which is quick to seize the gentle heart,
seized this man for the beautiful body
taken from me — and the way of it still wounds me.

Love, which absolves no loved one from loving,
seized me so strongly with delight in him
that, as you see, it has not left me yet.

Love led the two of us to a single death.
Caina waits for the one who put out our lives."
These were the words they carried over to us.

When I had heard those wounded souls,
I bowed my face and held it down so long
that at last the poet said: "What are you thinking?"

When I answered, I began: "Oh —
how many sweet thoughts, how much longing
brought these two to the road of grief."

Then I turned back to them and spoke,
and began: "Francesca, what you suffer
makes me weep for sorrow and pity.

But tell me: in the time of the sweet sighs,
by what signs, and how, did Love let you
know the desires you only half-guessed?"

And she to me: "There is no greater pain
than to remember the happy time
in misery — and that your teacher knows.

But if you long so much to know
the first root of our love,
then I will be like one who weeps as she speaks.

One day, for pleasure, we were reading
of Lancelot, how love had taken hold of him.
We were alone, and suspected nothing.

When we read how the longed-for smile
was kissed by such a lover,
this man, who never will be parted from me,

kissed me on the mouth, trembling all over.
A Galeotto was that book, and the one who wrote it.
That day we read in it no further."

While the one spirit said this,
the other wept so hard that out of pity
I fainted, as if I were dying,
and I fell as a dead body falls.

books.label: Inferno: Canto VI
paragraphs:
When my mind came back to itself —
it had shut down before the pity of those two
relatives, who left me lost in sorrow —

new torments and new tormented souls
rose up around me, wherever I moved,
whichever way I turned, whatever I looked at.

I am in the third circle now, the circle
of rain — eternal, cursed, cold, and heavy.
Its rule and its kind never change.

Cerberus, a cruel and monstrous beast,
barks like a dog out of three throats
over the people sunk in the muck.

And my guide reached out with both hands,
scooped up the earth, and with his fists full
threw it down into those ravenous throats.

Like a dog that barks and barks with hunger
but goes quiet the moment it has food to gnaw,
straining and fighting only to swallow it down —

that was how those filth-smeared muzzles went,
those jaws of the demon Cerberus, whose roar
leaves the souls wishing they were deaf.

We walked on across the shades the heavy rain
beats down, and we set our feet
on their emptiness, which looks like a real body.

Every one of them lay flat on the ground,
except for one, who sat straight up
the instant he saw us passing in front of him.

"You there, being led through this Hell,"
he said to me, "recognize me, if you can.
You were made before I was unmade."

And I to him: "The agony you're in
may be what blots you out of my memory,
so that it seems I've never seen you before.

But tell me who you are, to be set
in a place so wretched, in such a punishment
that if some are worse, none is more revolting."

And he to me: "Your city — so full
of envy now that the sack runs over —
held me inside it in the bright life above.

You citizens used to call me Ciacco.
For the ruinous sin of gluttony
I lie here, as you see, beaten down by the rain.

I answered him: "Ciacco, your suffering
weighs on me so it brings me to tears.
But tell me, if you know, what will become

of the citizens of that divided city?
Is there a single just man left? And tell me
why so much strife has torn it apart."

And he to me: "After long quarreling
they'll come to blood, and the party from the woods
will drive the other out with brutal force.

Then within three years that side must fall
in turn, and the first will rise again
by the power of one who now plays both shores.

For a long while it will hold its head high,
keeping the other crushed under heavy loads,
however much it weeps and rages at it.

The just are two, and no one there will hear them.
Pride, envy, and greed are the three sparks
that have set every heart on fire."

Here he brought his tearful words to an end.
And I to him: "I want you to teach me more —
give me the gift of a little more speech.

Farinata and Tegghiaio, who were so worthy,
Jacopo Rusticucci, Arrigo, Mosca,
and the others who set their minds on doing good —

tell me where they are, let me know them.
A great longing drives me to learn
whether Heaven sweetens them or Hell poisons them."

And he: "They are among the blackest souls.
A different sin drags them to the bottom.
If you go down far enough, you'll see them.

But when you are back in the sweet world,
I beg you, bring me to the minds of others.
No more will I tell you, no more will I answer."

Then he twisted his straight gaze to the side,
looked at me a moment, and bowed his head —
and fell with it, face down, among the other blind.

And my guide said to me: "He won't wake again
until the angel's trumpet sounds,
when the hostile Power comes at last.

Each one will find his miserable grave again,
will take back his flesh and his own shape,
will hear the verdict that thunders through eternity."

So we made our slow way across that foul
mixture of shades and rain, our steps dragging,
touching a little on the life to come.

And so I asked: "Master, this torment here —
after the great sentence is passed,
will it grow worse, or ease, or stay this fierce?"

And he to me: "Go back to your science,
which holds that the more perfect a thing is,
the more it feels of pleasure and of pain.

Even though these cursed people
can never come to true perfection,
they look to be more whole then than now."

We circled around that road, talking
of much more than I'll repeat here,
until we reached the point where the path drops down.
There we found Plutus, the great enemy.

books.label: Inferno: Canto VII
paragraphs:
said, to steady me: "Don't let your fear
harm you. Whatever power he may have,
he will not keep us from going down this rock."

Then he turned to that swollen, bloated face
and said: "Be quiet, you cursed wolf.
Feed on yourself, eat away at your own rage.

This descent into the dark is not without cause.
It is willed on high, there where Michael
took his vengeance on the proud rebellion."

The way sails, swollen with the wind,
collapse in a tangle when the mast snaps,
so the cruel beast fell to the ground.

And so we went down into the fourth ditch,
pushing on farther along the dismal shore
that bags up all the evil of the universe.

Justice of God! Who packs together so many
strange new toils and torments as I saw?
And why does our own guilt wreck us like this?

The way the wave there over Charybdis
breaks itself against the wave it runs into,
so here the people have to dance their round.

Here I saw more of them than anywhere else,
on one side and the other, with huge howls,
rolling great weights forward with their chests.

They crashed into each other, and right there
each one wheeled around, rolling back again,
shouting, "Why hoard?" and "Why throw it away?"

then each, when he reached his end of it,
turned through his half-circle to the next clash.
And I, with my heart all but pierced through,

said: "Master, explain it to me now —
who are these people? And were they all clerics,
these shaven crowns here on our left?"

And he to me: "Every one of them squinted
so badly in the mind, in the first life,
that they never spent with any measure.

Their voices bark it out clearly enough
when they come to the two points of the circle
where the opposite faults split them apart.

These were clerics, with no hairy covering
on the head — and popes, and cardinals,
in whom greed works its worst excess."

And I: "Master, among ones like these
I really ought to recognize a few
who were fouled with these same diseases."

And he to me: "You're chasing an empty thought.
The undiscerning life that made them filthy
now makes them too dim for anyone to know.

Forever they will come to these two collisions.
These will rise from the grave with fists clenched shut,
and these with the hair shorn off their heads.

Giving wrong and keeping wrong has cost them
the lovely world and set them in this brawl.
What that brawl is, I won't dress up in words.

Now you can see, my son, the brief charade
of the goods that are handed over to Fortune,
the ones the human race keeps fighting for.

All the gold that is under the moon,
or ever was, could not buy a moment's rest
for a single one of these worn-out souls."

"Master," I said to him, "tell me this too:
this Fortune you bring up — what is she,
who holds the world's goods so tight in her claws?"

And he to me: "O foolish creatures,
how deep the ignorance is that wounds you!
Now I want you to take in my judgment of her.

He whose knowledge surpasses everything
made the heavens and gave them guides,
so that every part shines on every part,

spreading the light out in equal measure.
In the same way, for the splendors of the world,
he set a general minister and guide

So one nation triumphs and another
withers, all by the verdict she hands down,
hidden the way a snake is hidden in grass.

Your knowledge has no defense against her.
She foresees, she judges, she carries out
her reign, the way the other gods rule theirs.

Her shiftings never come to any truce.
Necessity keeps driving her at speed,
so fast does one man's turn keep coming round.

And this is the one so often nailed to the cross
by the very people who ought to praise her,
who blame her wrongly and give her a bad name.

But she is in bliss, and does not hear them.
With the other first creatures, glad, she turns
her sphere, and rejoices in her own happiness.

Now let's go down to a greater sorrow.
Already every star is sinking that was rising
when I set out, and we are not allowed to linger."

We crossed the circle to the other bank,
beside a spring that boils and pours itself
down a channel that drains away from it.

The water was far darker than deep purple,
and we, keeping company with the murky waves,
made our way down by a rough, broken path.

When it has gone down to the foot
of the gray malignant slopes, this dreary stream
makes a marsh, and the marsh is named the Styx.

And I, who stood there straining to see,
made out people in that bog, smeared with mud,
all of them naked, all with furious looks.

They struck at each other, not with hands alone,
but with their heads, their chests, their feet,
and tore each other to pieces with their teeth.

The good master said: "Son, now you see
the souls of those whom anger overcame.
And I want you to know this for certain too:

down under the water there are people sighing,
and they make it bubble up at the surface,
as your eye tells you wherever it turns.

Stuck in the slime they say, 'We were sullen
in the sweet air that the sun makes glad,
carrying a lazy smoke inside ourselves.

Now we are sullen here in the black mire.'
This hymn they gurgle down inside their throats,
because they cannot get the words out whole."

So we went on around the filthy swamp,
in a wide arc between the dry bank and the bog,
our eyes on those who were gulping down the mud —
and we came at last to the foot of a tower.

books.label: Inferno: Canto VIII
paragraphs:
I should say, going on, that long before
we had reached the foot of the high tower,
our eyes had gone up to its top,

because of two small flames we saw set there,
and another, far off, signaling back,
so far that the eye could barely catch it.

And I turned to that sea of all understanding
and said: "What does this one say? And what reply
does that other fire give? Who lit them?"

And he to me: "Out across the murky waves
you can already make out what is coming,
if the marsh-fog doesn't hide it from you."

No bowstring ever drove an arrow from itself
that cut through the air so fast
as the little boat I saw in that moment,

coming toward us over the water,
under the steering of a single pilot,
who was shouting, "Now you're caught, vicious soul!"

"Phlegyas, Phlegyas, you cry out for nothing
this time," said my lord. "You'll have us
only long enough to cross the swamp."

Like a man who hears of some great trick
that has been played on him, and then seethes,
so Phlegyas seethed in his gathered rage.

My guide stepped down into the boat,
and then he had me get in after him,
and only when I entered did it sit low in the water.

As soon as my guide and I were aboard,
the ancient prow moves off, cutting
more of the water than it does for others.

While we were running across the dead channel,
one rose up in front of me, caked in mud,
and said, "Who are you, coming before your hour?"

And I to him: "If I come, I do not stay.
But who are you, gone so foul?"
He answered: "You see I am one who weeps."

And I to him: "With your weeping and your wailing,
you cursed spirit, stay right where you are,
for I know you, filthy as you are."

Then he reached both his hands toward the boat,
but my wary master shoved him back,
saying, "Get away there, with the other dogs!"

Then he put his arms around my neck,
kissed my face, and said: "Disdainful soul,
blessed is the woman who carried you.

In the world that one was an arrogant man.
No good deed adorns his memory,
so here his shade is wild with fury.

How many up there are taken for great kings
who will lie here like pigs in the muck,
leaving nothing behind but contempt!"

And I: "Master, I would dearly love
to see him ducked down into this sludge
before we make it out of the lake."

And he to me: "Before the far shore
comes into view, you'll be satisfied.
It's only right you should enjoy that wish."

A little after, I watched the people of the mud
tear into him with such fury
that to this day I praise and thank God for it.

They were all screaming, "Get Filippo Argenti!"
and that raging Florentine spirit
turned his teeth against his own flesh.

We left him there — I'll tell no more of him.
But a sound of grief struck against my ears,
and I strained my eyes wide ahead.

And the good master said: "Now, my son,
the city is coming close whose name is Dis,
with its grim citizens, its great throng."

And I: "Master, I can already see
its mosques there, plainly, down in the valley,
glowing red as if they'd come out of fire."

And he to me: "The eternal fire
that burns inside them turns them red,
as you can see, here in lower Hell."

Then we came inside the deep moats
that wall that desolate city all around.
The ramparts looked to me to be of iron.

Not without making a wide circuit first,
we came to a place where the pilot
bellowed at us, "Out — here is the entrance."

Over the gates I saw more than a thousand
rained down from Heaven, who in their fury
were saying, "Who is this, with no death in him,

who walks through the kingdom of the dead?"
And my knowing master made a sign
that he wished to speak with them in private.

Then they held back a little of their great scorn
and said: "You come alone. Let him go —
the one who's pushed so boldly into this realm.

Let him go back alone on his crazed road.
Let him try, if he can. You will stay here,
you who have led him through such dark country."

Imagine, reader, how I sank
at the sound of those accursed words,
for I believed I would never come back.

"O my dear guide, who more than seven times
have handed me back my safety, and drawn me
out of the dangers standing in my path,

don't leave me wrecked like this," I said.
"And if going on is forbidden us,
let's turn back together, and quickly."

And that lord, who had brought me there,
said to me: "Don't be afraid. No one
can take our crossing — it is granted by One above.

But wait for me here, and feed your worn spirit,
comfort it with a better hope,
for I will not abandon you in this low world."

So he goes off and leaves me there,
my sweet father, and I am left in doubt,
with Yes and No at war inside my head.

I couldn't hear what he proposed to them,
but he had not stood with them long
before each one scrambled back inside, racing.

They slammed the gates, those enemies of ours,
in my lord's face — and he was left outside,
and turned to me with slow, dragging steps.

His eyes were on the ground, his brow stripped
of all its boldness, and he said with sighs:
"Who has shut the houses of grief against me?"

And to me: "Don't you be afraid
because I'm angry — I will win this trial,
whatever they scheme up for defense inside.

This arrogance of theirs is nothing new.
They tried it once at a less hidden gate,
which stands to this day without a lock.

Over it you saw the inscription of death.
And already this side of it, coming down the slope,
crossing the circles with no escort,
is one by whose power the city will be opened."

books.label: Inferno: Canto IX
paragraphs:
The color that my cowardice had painted
over my face, seeing my guide turn back,
made him the quicker to swallow his own.

He stopped and listened hard, like a man straining,
because his eyes could carry him no distance
through the black air and the thick fog.

"Still, we have to win this fight," he began —
"unless . . . But such a one offered her help . . .
Oh, how I wish that someone would arrive!"

I saw clearly how he covered the beginning
of what he'd said with what came after it,
so that the end ran counter to the start —

but his words frightened me all the same,
because I drew out of the broken phrase
a worse meaning, maybe, than he meant.

"Down into this sad pit of a shell,
does anyone ever come from the first ring,
where the only punishment is hope cut off?"

This was my question, and he answered me:
"It rarely happens that one of us
makes the journey I am making now.

It's true that once before I came down here,
conjured by that pitiless Erichtho,
who called the shades back into their dead bodies.

My flesh had been stripped from me a short while
when she sent me inside that wall to bring
a spirit out of the circle of Judas.

That is the lowest place, the darkest,
the farthest from the heaven that turns all things.
I know the road well — so set your mind at ease.

This marsh that breathes out such a monstrous stench
rings the whole city of grief around,
where now we cannot enter without rage."

And he said more, but I can't hold it in mind,
because my eyes had drawn me all the way
to the high tower with its red-flaming top,

where, in an instant, I saw rise straight up
the three infernal Furies, stained with blood,
who had the limbs of women and their look,

And he, who knew well the handmaids
of the queen of everlasting grief,
said to me: "Look at the fierce Furies.

That is Megaera, there on the left.
The one weeping on the right is Alecto.
Tisiphone is between them." Then he was still.

"Let Medusa come, and we'll turn him to stone!"
they all cried, looking down. "It was a bad day
we failed to avenge the assault of Theseus."

"Turn around, and keep your eyes shut tight,
because if the Gorgon shows herself and you look,
there'd be no climbing back up, ever."

So said the master, and he turned me himself,
and did not trust it to my own hands,
but sealed my eyes shut with his too.

O you who have sound and steady minds,
look hard at the teaching that hides itself
beneath the veil of these strange verses.

And now, across the muddy water, came
the crash of a sound so full of terror
that both the banks of the marsh were trembling.

It was just like a wind, turned violent
by the clash of opposing heats, that strikes
the forest and, holding nothing back,

rips the branches off, beats them down, sweeps them away,
and goes on in a proud cloud of dust,
putting the wild beasts and the shepherds to flight.

He freed my eyes and said: "Now aim the line
of your sight across that ancient scum,
over there, where the smoke is thickest."

The way frogs, before the snake that hunts them,
scatter every which way through the water
until each one is hunched down in the mud,

I saw more than a thousand ruined souls
fleeing before one who was crossing the Styx
on foot, his soles never touching the water.

He fanned that greasy air away from his face,
waving his left hand over and over in front of him,
and only that disgust seemed to weary him.

I saw at once that he was sent from Heaven,
and turned to my master, who made a sign
that I should stand quiet and bow to him.

Ah, how full of scorn he seemed to me!
He came to the gate, and with a little wand
he opened it, and nothing held against him.

"O you cast out of Heaven, despised people,"
he began on that hideous threshold,
"where does this arrogance of yours come from?

Why do you kick against that will
whose end can never be cut short,
and which has many times piled on your pain?

What good does it do to butt against the fates?
Your own Cerberus, if you remember,
still carries his chin and throat rubbed raw for it."

Then he turned back along the filthy road
and said no word to us, but wore the look
of a man gripped and driven by another care

than the one of whoever stands before him.
And we set our feet toward the city,
sure of ourselves now after those holy words.

We went in without any struggle,
and I, who was eager to see
what such a fortress holds inside,

once I was in, threw my eyes all around me,
and saw on every side a wide plain,
full of suffering and terrible torment.

The way it is at Arles, where the Rhone goes still,
or at Pola, near the Quarnaro gulf
that closes Italy in and bathes its edges,

All of their lids had been lifted off,
and out of them came such grievous laments
they sounded like the truly wretched and tortured.

And I said: "Master, who are all these people
buried inside these vaults, who make themselves
heard by their mournful sighing?"

And he to me: "Here are the arch-heretics,
with their followers from every sect, and the tombs
are loaded far more full than you would think.

Like is buried here together with like,
and the monuments burn hotter and less hot."
And then he turned to the right, and we passed
between the torments and the high parapets.

books.label: Inferno: Canto X
paragraphs:
Now my master goes along a hidden path
between the city wall and the tormented,
and I follow at his back.

"O highest power, who wheel me as you please
through these unholy circles," I began,
"speak to me, and satisfy my longing.

The people lying here in these tombs —
could they be seen? All the lids
are already lifted, and no one stands guard."

And he to me: "They will all be sealed
when they come back here from Jehoshaphat
with the bodies they left up above.

On this side they have their burial ground,
Epicurus and all his followers,
who make the soul die along with the body.

But the question you put to me
will be answered soon enough in here,
and so will the wish you keep to yourself."

And I: "Good guide, I don't hide my heart
from you, except to say less than I might —
and you yourself have inclined me to that."

"O Tuscan, you who go alive
through the city of fire, speaking so plainly,
be pleased to stop a moment in this place.

Your way of speaking makes it clear
you were born in that noble homeland
to which I was, perhaps, too much a scourge."

And he said to me: "Turn around. What are you doing?
Look at Farinata, who has risen there —
from the waist up you'll see the whole of him."

I had already fixed my eyes on his,
and he was rising, with his chest and brow erect,
as if he held all Hell in great contempt.

And my guide's hands, bold and quick,
pushed me toward him between the tombs,
saying: "Let your words be clear and exact."

As soon as I stood at the foot of his tomb,
he looked me over, and then, almost scornful,
asked me: "Who were your ancestors?"

Then he said: "They were fierce enemies
to me, to my forefathers, and to my party,
so that twice over I scattered them."

"If they were driven out, they came back —
from every side, both times," I answered him.
"But your people never quite learned that art."

weeping, he said: "If you go through this blind
prison by the height of your own genius,
where is my son? Why isn't he with you?"

And I to him: "I don't come on my own.
The one waiting over there leads me here —
perhaps to one your Guido held in disdain."

Suddenly standing bolt upright, he cried:
"What? You said held — held? Is he not still alive?
Does the sweet light no longer strike his eyes?"

When he saw that I had paused,
that I held back a moment before answering,
he fell flat again, and showed himself no more.

But that other, the great-souled one, at whose word
I had stayed, did not change his look,
nor move his neck, nor bend his side.

Picking up his first thread, he went on:
"If they have learned that art so badly,
it torments me more than this bed does.

But the face of the lady who reigns down here
will not be rekindled fifty times
before you'll know the weight of that art yourself.

And as you hope to return to the sweet world,
tell me: why is that people so merciless
against my line in every one of its laws?"

And I to him: "The slaughter and the carnage
that stained the Arbia red
makes such prayers be said in our temple."

Then, having shaken his head with a sigh,
he said: "There I was not alone,
nor surely without cause did I move with the rest.

But I was alone, there where every one of them
agreed to wipe Florence off the earth —
I was the one who defended her openly."

"Ah, so may your seed find rest one day,"
I begged him, "untie this knot for me
that has tangled up my thinking here.

It seems, if I hear you rightly, that you see
beforehand what time is bringing on,
but have some other way with the present."

When they draw near, or arrive, our minds
are blank; and unless someone brings us word,
we know nothing of your human state.

So you can understand that all our knowledge
will be dead from the very moment
the door of the future is shut."

and if I stood mute just now before answering,
tell him I did it because I was already
thinking of the error you have solved for me."

He said: "More than a thousand lie here with me.
Inside is the second Frederick,
and the Cardinal; of the rest I say nothing."

Then he hid himself; and I turned my steps
back to the ancient poet, turning over
that saying that had sounded like a threat.

He moved on, and as we went, he said:
"Why are you so lost in yourself?"
And I answered the question he had asked.

"Keep in your mind what you have heard
spoken against you," the sage commanded me.
"And now listen here," and he raised his finger:

"When you stand before the sweet light
of her whose lovely eyes see everything,
from her you'll learn the journey of your life."

Then he turned his feet to the left.
We left the wall and went toward the center,
along a path that cuts down into a valley
whose stench, even up there, turned the stomach.
